opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the big limitation was a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. In a lot of that earlier work, the classic setup was: you have some environment, say an Atari game or a MuJoCo simulator, and you learn a world model of it so that your agent can plan or train in imagination and be more sample efficient. That's really valuable research, and it showed world models could work. But if you think about it, you already had the environment. Someone had already built the simulator by hand. So the world model was essentially a compressed, approximate copy of something that existed, and its main benefit was efficiency. It wasn't giving you anything fundamentally new.

The deeper issue is that if what we ultimately want is generally capable agents, the bottleneck isn't really sample efficiency in one environment. It's the lack of rich, diverse environments to train in at all. Every environment has to be designed by people, which is expensive and slow, so you end up with a fairly narrow set of worlds. Agents trained in those tend to overfit to them and don't generalize well.

So what's been exciting for us is flipping that around. Instead of learning a model of an environment you already have, can you learn from huge amounts of data, like videos from the internet, and generate environments that never existed? Then the world model isn't just a cheaper stand-in for a simulator. It becomes a way to create an essentially unlimited curriculum of new worlds for agents to learn in. That's the shift: from world models as a tool for efficiency to world models as a source of open-ended training data. I think that's where a lot of the real potential is.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier world models mainly improved efficiency by approximating an existing simulator, but it does not state that they failed to make otherwise unsolvable tasks solvable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think if you look at a lot of the earlier world-model work, the Ha and Schmidhuber paper, Dreamer, a lot of that line of research, the setup was that you already had a simulator. You had Atari, or you had a MuJoCo environment, or DeepMind Control, and the world model was essentially learning a compressed version of something you could already run for free. And that was great for showing the idea works. You could train an agent in imagination, you could show sample efficiency gains, and you could evaluate everything cleanly because the ground truth environment was right there.

But I think the limitation is that it kind of misses the whole point of why you'd want a world model in the first place. If you already have the simulator, the world model is at best a slightly more efficient or slightly more convenient version of it. It's not actually giving you anything new. The really interesting case is the one where you don't have the environment. You have data, you have videos, you have observations of people doing things, but nobody has written a simulator for that, and realistically nobody ever will, because the world is too open-ended to hand-code.

The other thing is that those environments were narrow by design. You'd train a world model on one Atari game, or a handful of them, and it would learn that one game. It wasn't generalizing to new scenes or new dynamics, because it never had to. The data distribution was tiny. And so the whole paradigm sort of capped out at reproducing things we already had, rather than opening up environments we didn't.

So for me, the shift was really about asking, can you learn an interactive world from unstructured data at scale, without action labels, without a simulator in the loop? Because if you can do that, then the world model stops being a research curiosity that mirrors an existing benchmark, and starts being the thing that generates the environments agents get trained and evaluated in. That's a much bigger deal, and it's the thing the earlier setup just wasn't positioned to test.

r001.rationale: The response says that with an existing simulator, a world model was only a more efficient or convenient version and “not actually giving you anything new”; it contrasts this with enabling environments that lack a simulator. This communicates that the earlier setup did not make otherwise unsolvable tasks solvable.

astra-6.text:
I think the limitation is that you already had the environment, and then you were learning a model of it, typically to make training an agent more efficient. So you could learn inside the model instead of taking lots of expensive steps in the real environment. That’s useful, but you’re still constrained by the environments you already have.

What’s exciting is the possibility of using a world model to create environments you didn’t have access to in the first place. Can you learn from videos, for example, and turn that into something an agent can interact with? Then the model isn’t just helping you solve an existing environment more efficiently—it’s opening up a much broader set of environments to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says world models made training in existing environments more efficient and were limited to those environments, but it does not state that they failed to make otherwise unsolvable tasks solvable.

sol-6.1.text: I think the limitation is that you already have the environment, so you can always go back and collect more data or test your policy in the real simulator. The world model is essentially a tool for making that process more efficient. That’s useful, but it doesn’t really address the question of what happens when you don’t have access to the environment in the first place. Can you learn a model from existing data that becomes an environment you can actually train an agent in? That’s a much more ambitious role for a world model.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models in the earlier setting as making data collection and policy testing more efficient, then contrasts that with learning to train without environment access. This communicates efficiency gains rather than making otherwise unsolvable tasks solvable.
